Empirical Research Plan: Governors’ Re-election Incentives and Fiscal Policy  

-------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (two-way fixed effects) complemented by an event-study.  
Why it fits:  
• The “treatment” (governor becomes ineligible for re-election because of a binding term limit) turns on and off within a state over time, but not at the same calendar year for all states (staggered adoption).  
• A DiD with state and year fixed effects therefore compares fiscal outcomes in the same state before vs. after the governor reaches the last term, while netting out common shocks and permanent state characteristics.  
• An event-study version allows visual and formal tests of the parallel-trends assumption and of dynamic effects (anticipation and post-exit fade-out).  

Robustness / auxiliary strategy:  
• Within–term-limited–states only (i.e., governors who face a two-consecutive-term cap). This makes the counterfactual governor more comparable (he/she also won once and is subject to exactly the same constitutional rules, just not yet in the last term).  
• Instrumental-variables robustness: instrument FinalTerm with TermLimitState × SecondTerm. This removes any residual selection on governors’ decision to seek the second term, but is not strictly necessary if the main DiD passes pre-trend tests.  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable: FinalTerm_st = 1 if in state s, year t, the sitting governor is constitutionally barred from seeking the next election (last allowable consecutive term); 0 otherwise.  
Control observations:  
• Same state in years when the governor is eligible (first term, or later terms in “no-limit” states).  
• Year t observations from other states whose governor is eligible.  
Treatment timing: First fiscal year that begins after the governor is sworn in for the final term; persists until the governor’s successor is inaugurated.  
No RDD running variable is used, so no cutoff applies.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Parallel trends: Absent the loss of re-election eligibility, treated and control state-years would have followed the same trend in taxes and spending. Plausible? Governors generally serve four-year terms with budgets largely shaped by macro conditions that can be captured by state and year fixed effects plus controls.  
A2. No anticipatory treatment effects: Fiscal policy is not changed in expectation of a coming final term more than (say) one year before. Plausible but testable with leads in the event study.  
A3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers): A governor’s term-limited status in State A does not affect fiscal choices in State B. Plausible given state autonomy.  
A4. Treatment exogeneity conditional on FE: Once we condition on governor fixed effects (or at least state × party) and macro controls, nothing else changes exactly when the governor hits the term limit. Reasonably plausible because the timing is dictated by constitutional rules.  
A5. No differential measurement error in outcomes across treated vs. control observations. Federal Census of Governments provides uniform measurement, so plausible.  

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigations  
T1. Selection into treatment: Only governors who have already won re-election can be in a “final” term; those governors may be systematically different (more popular, more skilled).  
   • Mitigation: Include governor fixed effects or restrict sample to states with binding two-consecutive-term limits and compare a governor’s own first vs. second term.  
T2. Partisan or legislative environment changes with treatment: Final-term governors might coincide with co-partisan control of the legislature, confounding the effect.  
   • Mitigation: Control for partisan composition of each chamber and for divided-government dummies; run models with state × year-of-gubernatorial-cycle fixed effects.  
T3. Simultaneous institutional reforms (tax or expenditure limitations, balanced-budget amendments) correlate with term-limit adoption.  
   • Mitigation: Include state-specific linear or quadratic time trends; re-estimate on the balanced‐budget–mandate-constant subsample; add controls for TELs (Tax & Expenditure Limits) and other institutions.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# -------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast FE regressions and Sun & Abraham estimator
library(broom)       # tidy output

# -------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
dat <- read_csv("state_panel_data.csv")  # assumes wide panel with one row per state–year

# -------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    # Indicator =1 if governor is in last allowable consecutive term
    FinalTerm = if_else(bind_term_limit == 1 & term_number == max_terms_allowed, 1, 0),
    
    # controls
    log_inc_pc   = log(real_income_per_capita),
    log_pop      = log(population),
    unem_rate    = unemployment_rate,
    
    # outcomes (examples)
    log_tot_tax  = log(total_taxes_pc),
    log_tot_exp  = log(total_expenditure_pc),
    log_welfare  = log(welfare_exp_pc)
  )

# -------------------------------
# 3. Main DiD specification
fe_main <- feols(log_tot_tax ~ FinalTerm + log_inc_pc + log_pop + unem_rate | state + year,
                 data = dat, cluster = ~state)
summary(fe_main)

# -------------------------------
# 4. Event-study using Sun & Abraham (staggered DiD)
# Assume variable 'years_since_final' already constructed (-4…+4, with -1 omitted)
dat <- dat %>% mutate(treat_year = if_else(FinalTerm == 1, start_year_final_term, NA_integer_))
fe_event <- feols(log_tot_tax ~ sunab(treat_year, year) + log_inc_pc + log_pop + unem_rate |
                    state + year,
                  data = dat, cluster = ~state)
iplot(fe_event)     # pre-trend graph

# -------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: within-term-limited-states only, governor FE
limited_states <- dat %>% filter(term_limit_const == 1)
fe_robust <- feols(log_tot_tax ~ FinalTerm + log_inc_pc + log_pop + unem_rate |
                     governor_id + year,          # governor fixed effects
                   data = limited_states, cluster = ~state)
summary(fe_robust)
```

6. Expected Results  
Theory of electoral accountability predicts that once re-election pressure disappears, incumbents may revert toward their intrinsic preferences—often thought to be higher spending and taxation than voters prefer. Therefore:  
• Direction: FinalTerm expected to raise total taxes per capita and total expenditures per capita; welfare spending should rise the most.  
• Magnitude (rough guess): +2–4 percent of the baseline outcome, i.e., roughly $70–$150 per capita in 2019 dollars on total spending; smaller but positive for taxes.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)  
C1. Parallel trends verified with pre-treatment leads: 1  
C2. No anticipation beyond one year: 0.5 (needs testing)  
C3. No spillovers across states: 1  
C4. No time-varying confounders correlated with treatment after controls: 0.5  
C5. Consistent measurement of outcomes across states/years: 1  

Total = 4 / 5 → Reasonably strong design, conditional on passing pre-trend tests.
